executive_summary: The US Dollar Index stood at 101.91 on the 2026-10-30 close (ICE weights applied to that day's closes), up 0.43% over one month, 2.12% over three months, 3.75% over six months and 2.37% over a year, 0.7 points below its 12 October 52-week high of 102.59 [22]. That gain is a euro story: EUR/USD fell 0.67% in October to 1.11674, while the dollar lost 4.49% to the krone, 2.29% to the krona, 1.79% to the Canadian dollar and 1.50% to sterling, so on an equal-weighted G10+SGD basis it weakened about 1.3% in the month. The narrative is a hiking Fed in an energy shock: the FOMC held 3.75-4.00% on 28 October by 10-2 with Cook and Hammack voting to hike, and futures price a December hike at 77-85% [1][3][4]. Growth is running hot, with third-quarter GDP at 3.4% annualised and the S&P Global composite PMI at 57.6 against 51.9 in the euro area, but inflation is not cooling: September core PCE was 3.1% y/y and headline CPI 3.7% [6][7][8][11]. Valuation is full but not extreme: the BIS real broad index is 107.11, the 21st percentile of its range since January 2024, while GDP-based PPP puts the dollar 26% rich against the euro and 62% rich against the yen [39][40]. The tension is that the dollar's carry is the third highest in G10+SGD at 3.875% and the US front end still yields 153-271bp over Germany, Japan, Canada and Sweden, yet every one of those gaps narrowed in October as peers turned hawkish, and the market prices the Fed path near 4.7% by September 2027 against a median dot of 4.1% [3][13]. Tactically we are Bullish (score +0.326, conviction 3, rank 1 of 11), looking for 102.80 by late November as a December hike stays priced, year-end funding tightens and reserves fall below $2.9tn [15]. Strategically we are Neutral (score -0.096, conviction 2, rank 6 of 11): peer tightening, a 3.0%-of-GDP current account deficit and a 6.2%-of-GDP budget deficit offset the carry, and our six-month DXY base case of 101.60 is close to spot but above the 101.12 forward [33][36].

tactical.analysis: The FOMC held the target range at 3.75-4.00% on 28 October by 10-2, with Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissenting in favour of an immediate 25bp hike, one meeting after the 16 September hike [1][3]. At a 3.875% mid-point the Fed ranks 3rd of 11 in G10+SGD, 72.5bp below the RBA and 62.5bp below Norges Bank, but 137.5bp above the ECB and the Bank of Canada, 262.5bp above the BoJ and 387.5bp above the SNB. The market prices the next move as a hike: fed funds futures put the probability of 4.00-4.25% on 9 December at 77.3% on the 30 October close and about 85% after Chair Warsh's press conference, with an implied post-meeting rate near 4.06-4.09% [3][4]. The 2-year Treasury at 4.61% on 29 October is 74bp above the policy mid-point, so the front end already discounts roughly one more hike and part of a second, and the 10-year at 4.98% gives a 2s10s slope of +38bp [12][13]. Front-end spreads remain wide, with the US 2-year 153bp over Germany, 271bp over Japan, 125bp over Canada and 187bp over Sweden, which keeps the carry channel open for the next four weeks. The data calendar is skewed towards confirming the hike: September core PCE of 3.1% y/y and third-quarter GDP of 3.4% annualised give the Committee little reason to retreat, and only a very weak payroll print on 6 November would challenge 77% pricing [6][7]. Our own probability for December is 70%, slightly below the market, because the September payroll gain of 29,000 and the 60,000 of downward revisions show a labour market that is cooling [9]. On balance the rate channel is dollar-positive tactically because the hike is likely and the front-end premium over the euro, yen, franc and krona is large, even though most of the move is priced.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the question is not whether the Fed hikes once more but how the dollar's rate advantage evolves while every peer except the SNB and Norges Bank is tightening. The September projections put the median funds rate at 4.1% for end-2026 and 4.1% for end-2027, one more hike and then a hold, while futures reported after the press conference price close to 4.7% by September 2027, roughly two further hikes beyond December [3]. That 50-60bp gap between the dots and the market is the main strategic mispricing: we side with the dots because core PCE is projected to fall to 2.5% in 2027 and Pantheon expects easing from mid-2027 [3][5]. Peers are closing the gap: the BoE is expected to hike on 5 November, the ECB and the BoJ are likely to hike in December, the RBNZ is weighing a hike to 3.00%, and the Riksbank is expected to move to 2.00% on 4 November [5]. October already showed that convergence, as the US 2-year premium narrowed 7bp against Germany, 21bp against Japan, 30bp against Canada and 24bp against Sweden. If the Fed stops at 4.00-4.25% while the ECB reaches 2.75-3.00% and the BoJ 1.50-1.75%, the dollar's spread to the euro and the yen narrows by 25-50bp by April 2027. The carry still pays: at 137.5bp against the euro and 262.5bp against the yen it remains among the highest in the group, and the long end at 4.98% keeps Treasuries attractive to foreign buyers. We therefore hold Neutral: a wide but narrowing differential and a market path that already exceeds the Fed's own projections offset the carry income.

carry_analysis.carry_regime: Carry is working for the dollar against low-yielders: the dollar gained 3.27% against the euro and 4.68% against the New Zealand dollar over three months while earning 112.5-137.5bp. It is not working against higher- or similar-yielders with commodity support, where the dollar lost 4.49% to the krone and 1.45% to the Australian dollar in October. All ratios are carry over 60-day realised volatility; implied-volatility ratios using CME one-month at-the-money volatility are 0.23 against the euro (5.88%) and 0.37 against the yen (7.16%) [27].
carry_analysis.breakeven_move: Long USD against the euro earns about 154 pips a year at 1.11674: EUR/USD can rise 13 pips in a month, 38 pips in three months or 77 pips in six before the carry is erased. Against the yen the cushion is about 0.35 yen a month and 2.07 yen over six months; against the franc about 27 pips a month.

tactical.analysis: US growth is running well above trend: the advance estimate put third-quarter real GDP at 3.4% annualised, up from 2.2%, with real final sales to private domestic purchasers at 4.9%, and the Atlanta Fed tracks the fourth quarter at 3.2-3.3% [5][6]. Inflation is elevated and the composition argues for persistence: September PCE prices rose 0.5% m/m and 3.6% y/y, core PCE 0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y, and the Fed's 2% target is 110bp away on its preferred measure [7]. CPI tells the same story with an energy shock on top: headline CPI rose 0.6% m/m to 3.7% y/y on a 5.2% jump in energy, while core CPI was 2.6% y/y with a three-month annualised pace of 3.4% [8]. The drivers are mainly cost-push from energy, with Brent up about 15% in October, but services ex energy at 3.1% y/y and ISM prices paid at 77.9 show second-round pressure building [8][10][29]. The labour market is the soft spot: September payrolls rose only 29,000, July and August were revised down by 60,000, unemployment rose to 4.2% and average hourly earnings grew 3.0% y/y, below inflation [9]. Leading indicators remain strong, with ISM manufacturing at 54.5, new orders at 55.3 and the S&P Global flash composite PMI at 57.6 against 51.9 in the euro area, a 5.7-point growth lead that is the core of the exceptionalism case [10][11]. Consensus for 6 November is +55,000 payrolls and 4.2% unemployment; we expect 40,000-70,000, so the risk of a downside surprise large enough to unwind December pricing is limited [5]. For the next four weeks strong activity plus sticky inflation keeps the Fed hawkish and the growth differential with Europe wide, which is dollar-positive.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices growth near 3% and core PCE stuck above 3%, which is why December is 77-85% priced. The surprise risk is asymmetric to the downside only in payrolls; activity and price surveys point to firm prints, and the October CPI on 10 November is more likely to confirm than to undermine the hike.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the US retains a growth lead over the large economies that dominate the dollar index: GDP growth of 2.07% y/y compares with 1.3% in the euro area, 0.73% in Japan, 1.37% in the UK and 0.95% in Canada, and its 0.83% quarterly pace is the third highest in G10+SGD after Switzerland and Singapore, although Sweden, Switzerland and New Zealand grow faster on a yearly basis. Productivity is carrying the expansion, which the FOMC statement called strong, and capital investment linked to AI remains robust, so potential growth looks higher than in previous cycles [1]. Inflation is likely to stay above target through mid-2027: the Fed projects core PCE at 3.4% for 2026 and 2.5% for 2027, and with Brent above US$110 the energy pass-through has further to run [3][29]. Third-quarter core PCE rose only 2.5% annualised, down from 3.3%, which suggests the underlying trend is improving even as the monthly pace has picked up again [6]. The weak spot is employment: three-month average payroll growth is about 51,000 and real average hourly earnings fell 0.7% y/y, so consumer spending relies on a 3.8% saving rate that has little room to fall further [7][8][9]. Consumer sentiment is depressed, with the Michigan index at 48.0 and one-year inflation expectations at 4.7%, a combination that points to slower real consumption in the first half of 2027. Even so, a slowdown from 3.4% to 2% would leave the US growing faster than Europe and Japan, so the relative growth signal remains dollar-positive. We are Bullish with lower confidence than tactically because the labour market could crack, and a rise in unemployment to 4.5% would shift the Fed's reaction function quickly.

tactical.analysis: Risk appetite turned more cautious at the end of October: the VIX closed at 17.2 on 29 October, the 52nd percentile of a year, and traded at 20.05 midday on 30 October as the S&P 500 fell 1.8% and the Nasdaq 3.5% on disappointing technology earnings [4][30]. The S&P 500 finished 30 October in a 7,580-7,623 range (best available, flagged: sources differ on the close), about 2.8% below its October record of 7,844.67 and roughly 11% higher over a year [30]. Credit has widened quietly: the US investment-grade option-adjusted spread is 89bp, the 96th percentile of a year, and high yield 326bp, the 95th percentile, up 5bp and 18bp in a month [31]. The regime is transitioning from risk-on to cautious, driven by doubts over AI capital spending, an oil shock and the prospect of US strikes on Iran after the midterms [29]. On the dollar smile the US sits on the right side, with exceptional growth, while the energy war and widening credit spreads pull towards the left side, which should be dollar-positive in theory. In practice the dollar did not rally on the 30 October sell-off: the DXY fell from 102.04 to 101.91 that day as the yen and franc absorbed haven demand and gold fell 3.6%, so the dollar's safe-haven beta is currently weak [29]. US equities still outperform: the S&P 500 is up about 11% over a year against a euro area economy whose PMI is 5.7 points weaker, which keeps foreign equity inflows supportive [11]. With the haven channel muted and the growth channel positive, we hold the factor Neutral tactically, awaiting evidence that a risk-off shock lifts the dollar rather than the yen.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the risk factor is two-sided for the dollar. A deeper AI-led equity correction would hit US assets first, because the US accounts for most of the AI capital spending that has driven the S&P 500 to records, and that would weaken the US-exceptionalism side of the smile [30]. At the same time, an escalation in the Gulf after the midterms or a disorderly widening in credit would push the dollar to the left side of the smile, where funding demand and Treasury buying typically dominate [29]. The two shocks are partly correlated, which makes the net effect hard to sign: an oil spike above US$130 would damage European and Japanese terms of trade more than US ones, while an equity bust would reduce foreign demand for US stocks. Corporate credit spreads at 89bp investment-grade and 326bp high yield are wider than a year ago but still low relative to stress episodes, so the system has room to absorb shocks [31]. Real money is long US equities and underhedged on the currency, according to ING, so a risk-off move led by US assets could trigger dollar selling through higher hedge ratios [24]. That hedging channel is the main reason the dollar did not rally on the 30 October sell-off, and it would matter more in a prolonged correction than in a short shock. We therefore keep the strategic factor Neutral at lower confidence than tactically.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the flow picture leans against the dollar even though speculative positioning is only moderately long. The dollar's share of allocated reserves fell to 56.70% in Q2 2026 from 57.18% while the euro's share rose to 20.60%, and the IMF says valuation effects were limited, so the decline reflects allocation rather than price moves [35]. Foreign private investors remain heavy buyers of US securities, with net long-term purchases of USD 300.7bn in August, but foreign holdings of Treasury bills fell USD 47.8bn and official inflows were only USD 21.3bn [34]. ING identifies low hedge ratios on US assets as the main risk for the dollar, and with US equities 2.8% off their highs and the Fed near the end of its cycle, the incentive to raise hedge ratios grows as the rate differential narrows [24][30]. Raising hedge ratios means selling dollars forward without selling the underlying assets, which can weaken the dollar even when portfolio inflows continue. Speculative DXY length at the 57th-71st percentile of five years leaves room for further buying if the Fed surprises hawkishly, but the five-week build from -4,495 to +3,158 leveraged contracts has used up the clean short-covering fuel. Asset managers' USD 7.9bn net long in foreign currency futures is the stickier position, and it has held through the September-October dollar rally. We are Bearish strategically at modest confidence: reserve diversification and hedging flows are slow-moving negatives, offset only partly by strong private portfolio inflows.

factors.contrarian_analysis_tactical: Stretched for the dollar index begins near the 90th percentile of one year for leveraged funds, roughly +12,000 to +15,000 contracts; at +3,158 and the 87th percentile on a one-year basis, positioning is close to but not inside that zone, and on five years it is only the 71st percentile. An unwind would most plausibly come from a payroll print below zero on 6 November, a soft October CPI on 10 November or a Democratic sweep on 3 November that revives tariff risk, each of which would cut December pricing [5][24]. The squeeze would be modest: the five-week build of about 7,600 contracts is small next to the five-year range of 51,500 contracts, so we would expect a 0.8-1.2% DXY setback rather than a disorderly move. The contrarian case is that the consensus long dollar is a rate trade with a short shelf life, and the real-money euro and yen longs show the other side is still positioned for the dollar to weaken. As a signal, current positioning is neutral: it neither offers short-covering fuel nor is crowded enough to fade.
factors.contrarian_analysis_strategic: On a six-month view the relevant crowding is not in futures but in unhedged foreign holdings of US assets, which ING flags as the main dollar risk [24]. If the Fed's last hike comes in December and the market's 4.7% path for 2027 is repriced towards the 4.1% median dot, the hedging cost falls by 25-50bp and the incentive to hedge rises. A historical analogue is the period after the end of a Fed tightening cycle, when the dollar typically weakened as hedge ratios rose rather than as assets were sold. The contrarian case for the dollar is that a hawkish surprise to 4.50% by March would widen the carry and force asset managers to cut their USD 7.9bn foreign-currency long. On balance positioning and flows are a mild bearish signal over six months.

tactical.analysis: The US current account deficit widened to USD 246.0bn, 3.0% of GDP, in Q2 2026 from USD 212.6bn and 2.7% in Q1, with a larger goods deficit only partly offset by narrower primary and secondary income deficits [33]. Monthly trade data point to further widening: the August trade deficit was USD 105.6bn against USD 92.8bn in July, and the advance September goods deficit was USD 134.9bn. The terms of trade are moving in the US favour because the country is a net energy exporter: WTI settled at US$104.12 and Brent at US$117.64 on 30 October, up about 12% and 15% in the month, while Henry Hub spot gas is only US$2.76 [29]. That oil shock damages the euro area, Japan and Singapore far more than the US, but it helps the krone and the Canadian dollar more than the dollar, which is why the dollar lost 4.49% to the krone in October. Capital flows are strong: foreigners bought a net USD 300.7bn of long-term US securities in August and the total TIC inflow was USD 199.8bn, enough to finance the current account several times over [34]. Trade policy is the swing factor: refunds of about USD 130bn of the USD 166bn in eligible tariffs were paid from May to September, and a change of House control could shift trade policy again [24][36]. Over four weeks these forces largely net out against the G10 average: positive terms of trade and inflows against the euro and yen, negative against the petro-currencies. We hold the factor Neutral tactically.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the external balance is a structural drag on the dollar. The current account deficit of 3.0% of GDP is the largest in absolute terms in the world and the third largest relative to GDP in G10+SGD after Australia (3.67%) and New Zealand (3.26%), and the September goods deficit of USD 134.9bn suggests Q3 will be wider [33]. The net international investment position deteriorated by USD 1.15tn in a single quarter to -USD 22.42tn, so the US must attract ever larger capital inflows to sustain the dollar [33]. Twin deficits are widening together, with the federal deficit at 6.2% of GDP in FY2026, which historically accelerates dollar weakness once the rate advantage stops widening [36]. Reserve managers are already diversifying, with the dollar's COFER share down 48bp in a quarter to 56.70% [35]. Against this, the energy shock improves US terms of trade relative to every major importer, and an oil price above US$100 recycles petrodollars into US assets. Private inflows of USD 257.8bn in August show that the deficit is financed comfortably for now, which is why the deficit has not weighed on the dollar this year [34]. We are Bearish at modest confidence: the deficit is financed while US yields are 4.6-5.0%, but as peers raise rates the required compensation rises and the balance shifts against the dollar.

tactical.analysis: The 28 October statement was hawkish in tone: it said inflation 'remains elevated', described activity as 'expanding at a strong pace', upgraded from 'solid', and ended with 'The Committee will deliver price stability' [1][5]. Two governors, Cook and Hammack, dissented for an immediate hike, so the hawkish wing of the Committee is visible and voting [1]. Chair Warsh, at his press conference, declined to pre-judge December and said he does not believe in forward guidance outside a crisis, which removes the explicit signalling the market relied on under his predecessor [3]. He also said he was not uncomfortable with tighter financial conditions and that it is the Fed's responsibility to get inflation down after close to six years above goal [3][5]. The market has accepted the hawkish message: December pricing rose to about 85% after the press conference before settling at 77.3% on 30 October, above the 12-of-18 majority that projected one more hike in September [3][4]. The gap between the Fed's projected path and market pricing is therefore positive for December but already wide beyond it, with futures near 4.7% by September 2027 against a median dot of 4.1% [3]. The next communication events are the minutes on 18 November and a speech by Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman on 6 November, and the minutes will show how close the October decision was [20]. With hawkish language balanced by the absence of guidance and pricing already ahead of the dots, we hold the factor Neutral tactically.

strategic.analysis: Over six months credibility is the Fed's strongest asset and its main question mark. The Committee has delivered on its words: it hiked on 16 September, held with hawkish dissents in October and kept the 'deliver price stability' commitment, which supports the dollar against central banks that are only now turning hawkish [1]. Inflation has been above target for close to six years, however, and the September projections show core PCE at 3.4% this year, so the Fed's credibility rests on actually reaching 2.5% in 2027 [3]. Chair Warsh's rejection of forward guidance increases meeting-by-meeting volatility and makes the 9 December projections, the first under the new approach, the key strategic signal [3]. The political context is supportive for now: Treasury Secretary Bessent said further hikes would not necessarily be mistakes, which reduces the risk that the administration openly pressures the Fed before the 2027 decisions [5]. After the midterms, a Democratic House would increase oversight of the Fed but would not change its leadership, so we see little direct change to independence risk. The longer-run dot at 3.2% shows the Committee expects to cut eventually, and the market's 4.7% path for late 2027 is closer to the hawkish dissenters than to the median, so a dovish repricing is the more likely surprise over six months [3]. We hold Neutral: the Fed is credible and hawkish, but the market already prices more than its median member and the absence of guidance makes the path uncertain.

tactical.analysis: The first binary event is the 3 November midterm election, in which all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are contested; Polymarket put the Democrats at 94% to win the House and 69% the Senate, with a Democratic sweep at 70% [5]. OFX's framework is that divided government is broadly neutral to modestly negative for the dollar, while a change of control in both chambers raises volatility and the risk of dollar weakness [32]. ING flags that a Republican loss of the House could push the administration back towards trade policy, which it sees as dollar-negative [24]. The second event is the Iran war, now in its ninth month: two tankers were struck in the Strait of Hormuz within 24 hours on 29-30 October, and the President said the US would not strike Iran before the midterms, leaving the period after 3 November open [29]. Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on 30 October, so the outcomes range from a deal that takes Brent below US$100 to strikes that take it above US$130 [29]. A strike would most likely lift the dollar against the euro, yen and Asian importers but weaken it against the krone and the Canadian dollar, so the G10-average effect is smaller than the headline. The third is US intervention policy: the joint Japan-US intervention when USD/JPY passed 160 in late July means the dollar's upside against the yen is managed by both governments, an unusual cap [26]. We assign about 20% to a US strike within four weeks and 15% to a ceasefire, and with the midterm result largely priced the factor is Neutral tactically.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the event map has three branches. Trade policy could return: ING expects a Republican loss of the House to push the administration towards trade actions, and tariffs have already been unwound in part, with about USD 130bn of refunds paid from May to September [24][36]. Renewed tariffs were dollar-positive in 2018 through terms of trade but dollar-negative in 2025 through confidence in US assets, so the sign is uncertain. The Gulf conflict could escalate or settle: a deal would remove the energy premium that has helped the dollar against the euro and yen, while a prolonged closure of Hormuz would deepen Europe's and Japan's terms-of-trade shock [29]. Fiscal deadlines could reappear with a divided Congress, which raises the chance of a government shutdown in 2027 and of brinkmanship over spending. Intervention coordination with Japan above 160 limits the dollar's upside in its second-largest index component [26]. Tail risks with more than 2% FX impact include a US-Iran deal (we estimate 25% within six months, DXY -1.5% to -2.5%), a sustained Hormuz closure (15%, DXY +2% against importers), and a broad tariff escalation (15%, sign uncertain). These offset each other, so we hold the factor Neutral.

tactical.analysis: The federal deficit was USD 2.0tn in FY2026, 6.2% of GDP, up from 5.8% in FY2025, as outlays grew 6% and revenue 3%, according to CBO's September budget review [36]. Debt held by the public is about USD 32.3tn, 100% of GDP, and interest costs reached about USD 1.1tn, 3.4% of GDP, roughly a fifth of federal revenue of USD 5.4tn [36][37]. Interest payments rose USD 115bn, or 11%, in a year, and customs receipts fell USD 22bn as about USD 130bn of tariffs were refunded from May to September [36]. The ratings are stable one notch below AAA: S&P affirmed AA+ in June, citing solid growth and credible monetary policy, and all three agencies carry stable outlooks [38]. The quarterly refunding on 4 November is the near-term supply event: Treasury borrowed USD 739bn in the third quarter and plans USD 628bn in the fourth, assuming an USD 850bn end-December cash balance, and the market will watch whether the promise to hold coupon sizes 'for at least the next several quarters' survives [5]. The 10-year at 4.98% and the 30-year at 5.32% sit at the 98th percentile of five years, so the bond market is charging a premium, but auctions are clearing and foreigners bought USD 300.7bn of long-term securities in August [12][34]. No free source publishes a US sovereign CDS spread, so the market's credit view is read from term yields instead. The next fiscal deadline is the 11 December expiry of the continuing resolution signed on 2 September, just beyond the four-week window, and with the refunding expected to be unchanged the fiscal factor is Neutral tactically [16].

A surprise increase in coupon guidance would lift long yields and steepen the curve, which in this regime is more likely to weaken the dollar through fiscal concern than strengthen it through yield.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the fiscal trajectory is a slow but real dollar negative. A deficit of 6.2% of GDP outside recession, interest costs at 3.4% of GDP and debt at 100% of GDP leave little room for fiscal support if growth slows, and the interest bill rises as low-coupon debt rolls over at 4.6-5.0% [36][37]. S&P noted that the rating could slip within two years if deficits rise because lawmakers cannot contain spending or manage the revenue effects of the tax code [38]. A Democratic House from January 2027 increases the odds of budget confrontations in 2027, and before that the lame-duck Congress must extend government funding that expires on 11 December [16]. The bond market has started to price this: the 30-year at 5.32% and the 10-year real yield at 2.63% are near the top of their five-year ranges, while 10-year breakevens are only 2.34%, so the premium is for term and fiscal risk rather than inflation [12]. Higher term premia have supported the dollar so far by raising yields, but a sharper fiscal premium would reverse that relationship, as it did for sterling in 2022. The tariff-refund episode, about USD 130bn of the USD 166bn eligible paid back from May to September, also shows that revenue measures can be reversed, which weakens the credibility of deficit projections [36]. strategic.analysis: Over six months the Fed is likely to respond to any reserve scarcity rather than let funding tighten. The implementation note authorises the Desk to buy bills, and coupons with up to three years to maturity, when appropriate to maintain ample reserves, and the New York Fed has said it expects reserves to stay ample near term even without purchases [2][17]. Reserve management purchases ran at USD 40bn a month and then USD 10bn before stopping in mid-August, so the Fed has a tested tool to add reserves if SOFR rises persistently above IORB [17]. Treasury's planned decline in the TGA to USD 850bn by end-December would return about USD 165bn of reserves from the 28 October level, easing conditions in early 2027 [5][15]. Bank lending conditions are not restrictive: the July survey showed C&I standards basically unchanged and CRE standards eased, though credit card and non-bank lending standards are tight [19]. On the dollar smile, liquidity is neither scarce enough to push the dollar to the left side nor abundant enough to push it to the bottom. Global dollar demand from energy importers paying more for oil is a mild support, while swap-line usage of USD 156m shows no strain [15]. We hold the strategic factor Neutral: tightness into year-end is likely to be met by renewed bill purchases, and the TGA decline adds liquidity after December.

cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: Mid-December 2026, between the 9 December FOMC projections and the 18 December BoJ decision, with year-end funding pressure fading in early January.
cross_horizon_consistency.catalyst_for_transition: December projections confirming a single further hike and a hold through 2027, combined with ECB and BoJ hikes on 17-18 December, would turn the tactical view Neutral and leave the strategic view Neutral to Bearish.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Hold tactical dollar longs against the euro and franc into the December FOMC and take profit into strength near 102.8-103.0; then rotate into strategic short-dollar relative value against the yen and krona after the BoJ meeting.

forward_vs_spot.interpretation: There is no listed DXY forward in free sources, so the index forward is the 30 October close carried at the index-weighted policy-rate differential of 1.52% a year (the Fed mid-point of 3.875% against a weighted 2.357% for the ECB, BoJ, BoE, BoC, Riksbank and SNB). EUR/USD forward points come from the CME euro futures roll of +145.9bp a year observed 29 October, consistent with the 137.5bp policy gap plus a small basis [27]. Forwards imply the dollar weakening 1.5% a year; our path has it firmer at every horizon, so the edge is positive for the dollar at one, three and six months, largest at one month (+1.02 points) and smallest at six (+0.48 points). Strategically that means a Neutral spot view still favours holding dollars forward, because the carry exceeds the expected spot decline.

key_catalysts.rationale: A 25bp hike to 4.00-4.25% is 77-85% priced; the projections decide whether the market's 4.7% path for 2027 survives. A hike with a hold signal is dollar-negative strategically; a hike with higher dots is dollar-positive.

key_catalysts.event: Expiry of the continuing resolution funding the US government
key_catalysts.rationale: The stopgap signed on 2 September expires on 11 December; a lapse would delay data and raise fiscal-risk premia, which in this regime weighs on the dollar.

key_catalysts.event: ECB decision with projections; BoE; Norges Bank Monetary Policy Report
key_catalysts.rationale: ING expects the ECB to match the Fed with a hike to 2.75%, narrowing the dollar's euro carry to 112.5bp; the BoE may hike again.
A hike to 1.50% would narrow the US-Japan policy gap to 250-275bp after the Fed's move and test USD/JPY below 155; intervention near 160 caps the other side.

key_catalysts.event: Year-end dollar funding and balance-sheet turn
key_catalysts.rationale: With reserves near USD 2.9tn and the TGA above USD 1tn, year-end demand for dollars should push SOFR above IORB and lift the cost of dollar funding for foreign borrowers until the TGA falls towards USD 850bn.
The first meeting after the projections tests whether the Fed holds at 4.00-4.25%; the market's 2027 path implies further hikes that we do not expect.
If core PCE has fallen towards 2.7%, the March projections are likely to confirm a hold and pull the 2027 path down towards the median dot of 4.1%.

invalidators.condition: If the DXY closes below its 50-day average of 100.81 for three sessions, would turn Neutral tactically because trend-following flows would reverse.

invalidators.quantitative_threshold: 2027 median dot 4.6% or higher; core PCE above 3.2%

invalidators.condition: If reserves fall below USD 2.75tn and the Fed restarts bill purchases of USD 40bn a month or more, would turn Bearish strategically because liquidity would be added to the system at scale.

invalidators.quantitative_threshold: Reserves below USD 2.75tn; purchases of USD 40bn a month or more

invalidators.condition: If a Democratic sweep on 3 November is followed by tariff escalation or a lapse in government funding on 11 December, would turn Bearish strategically because fiscal and policy risk premia would rise on US assets.

invalidators.quantitative_threshold: New tariffs of 10% or more on a major partner, or a funding lapse of more than three days

factors_changed.reason: Third-quarter GDP of 3.4% and a 5.7-point PMI lead over the euro area confirm a durable growth gap even as the labour market softens.
The dollar fell on the 30 October equity sell-off, so its haven response is no longer reliable.
The hawkish October statement is offset by Chair Warsh's refusal to give forward guidance and by market pricing already above the dots.
With the market path near 4.7% for September 2027 against a 4.1% median dot, the next surprise from Fed communication is more likely dovish than hawkish.
The midterm outcome is largely priced and the Iran war now cuts both ways for the dollar, helping it against the euro and yen while hurting it against oil exporters.
Reserves fell USD 68.8bn in a week to USD 2,893.8bn and the TGA rose above USD 1tn, tightening funding into year-end.
Reserve management purchases stopped in mid-August and the TGA is set to fall in December, so the liquidity drag and support roughly offset.

seasonality.pattern: Year-end brings seasonal demand for dollar funding and thinner liquidity, which typically firms the dollar and offshore funding costs in the second half of December before the pressure fades in early January; Japan's fiscal year-end in March brings repatriation flows that tend to support the yen against the dollar.
seasonality.historical_magnitude: We do not attach a reliable average return to either pattern; both are flow effects that shape the path within the scenarios rather than independent directional drivers.
seasonality.current_alignment: Year-end funding supports the tactical Bullish view and is captured in the Bullish USD Liquidity factor; March repatriation supports the strategic short USD/JPY relative-value view.

assumptions: The US Dollar Index is computed with the ICE formula from the 2026-10-30 closes of its six component pairs; spot levels, moving averages, 52-week ranges, percentiles and realised volatility are from weekday closing bars to 2026-10-30, with realised volatility annualised on 252 days.

The Fed policy rate is the 3.875% mid-point of the 3.75-4.00% target range; peer policy rates are the latest official decisions, including the Bank of Canada's 2.50% after its 28 October hike, and Singapore's short rate is three-month compounded SORA of 1.2970% because MAS has no policy rate.

Carry is the policy-rate differential; carry-to-volatility ratios use 60-day realised volatility of each pair; implied volatilities and 25-delta risk reversals are CME at-the-money quotes on euro and yen futures options observed 2026-10-29, and the implied-volatility percentile uses 41 observations since 23 August 2026 because a full year of quotes is not available.

December hike probabilities differ by source and time of day (77.3% at the 30 October close on a CME-method calculation, about 85% after the 28 October press conference, about 75% on 2 November); we use the 77-85% range and our own 70% estimate.

CFTC positioning is the ICE US Dollar Index futures report and the six CME currency futures for the week to 27 October; dollar-equivalent values convert contracts at 30 October spot, and percentiles use one-, three- and five-year windows of weekly reports.

There is no free source for 3-month EUR/USD or JPY/USD cross-currency basis, a US sovereign CDS spread or a current term-premium estimate; the dollar funding premium is inferred from CME futures rolls against policy gaps, which also embed expected policy changes.

PPP deviations use World Bank GDP PPP conversion factors as applied across G10+SGD this month (best available, flagged: the World Bank page did not display values on 2026-11-02); positive values mean the dollar is above parity.

The S&P 500 close for 30 October is shown as a 7,580-7,623 range because sources disagree (best available, flagged); FOMC dates in 2027 are given as weeks because the official dates were not confirmed for this report.
